8bef511e: Every blocker you can switch off yourself eventually gets switched off. Here are the setups that genuinely hold, and the trade-offs of each.

ccde53e6: How do I block apps so I can't unblock them?
92e5294d: Any block whose off switch you control will eventually be switched off. The two setups that genuinely hold are having another person set a passcode you never see, or using an app with a built-in approval flow where a trusted person approves each unlock remotely.
5617bea7: Can you bypass Apple Screen Time?
0fe4a2e8: You can lift your own Screen Time limits at any time because you hold the passcode. That is by design. It makes Screen Time useful as a speed bump but unreliable against a deliberate craving.
6d9e62fb: What is the strictest app blocker for iPhone?
a0dc2f6b: Strictness depends on who holds the off switch rather than on features. Blockers where another person approves each unlock are structurally stricter than any self-controlled mode, because no setting on your own phone can lift them.
366e1956: Should I block all my distracting apps at once?
de15ef60: No. Start with the single app you already know is the problem. Blocking several at once is the most common reason people abandon a blocker in the first two weeks.

91ef35c1: There is a specific test for whether a block will survive contact with a real craving: at the moment it fires, can you undo it alone?
127cf158: By Shuaib Khan · 6 min read · Updated August 2026
2d0c7e37: Most app blockers fail the same test. At the moment the block fires, you can undo it by yourself — a button, a passcode you know, a setting two taps away. Everything else about the app is irrelevant once that is true.
5bc260e6: So the useful question when comparing blockers is narrow: at the moment you most want in, is the decision still yours?
3a88c478: A pause, a breathing exercise, a "are you sure?" screen. Apps like one sec and ScreenZen do this deliberately well.
5e11f285: Holds against: unconscious reaching. Genuinely effective — a large share of phone pickups are automatic rather than intentional, and a two-second interruption kills them.
686d3022: Fails against: anything you actually decided to do. By design, you can always continue. That is the point of the category, not a flaw.
88439af8: A session you start, with a countdown. Forest and most focus timers work this way.
5c89042a: Holds against: distraction inside a work session you chose to start.
4b7c7868: Fails against: evenings and weekends, because you simply do not start a session. A timer you must opt into is only ever as reliable as the moment you opted in.
23e2e9da: Apple Screen Time and most strict modes. The block is real, and the code is yours.
6842a8b4: Holds against: mild impulse, and being asked adds a useful pause.
1663bf36: Fails against: deliberate craving. You know the code. This is the failure mode almost everyone hits.
16da6352: The decision genuinely leaves your hands. There are two versions worth distinguishing.
207712cd: The improvised version is having someone else type a passcode you never see. It works, and it costs nothing to try. Its weakness is logistical: they have to be physically present every time you have a legitimate reason to get in, which is why most people abandon it within a fortnight.
dff85658: The built-in version is an app with a request-and-approve flow, where you ask remotely and they answer in one tap. Same principle, without the logistics problem.
67799067: Be honest about which failure mode is yours. They need different tools.
c0b21b6c: You open apps without noticing. Friction is the right answer. You do not need anything stronger, and stronger will feel oppressive.
ac595274: You focus badly during work. A timer is enough, because you are present and willing at the start of the session.
bf3f0847: You lose whole evenings, deliberately, and regret it. Nothing you can undo alone will hold. This is the case that needs another person.
eeb34c0a: Most people over-apply the strict option to problems that only needed friction, then abandon the whole thing because it felt like a punishment. Match the tool to the actual failure.
cbd93bd7: If you have already broken your own limit on a specific app more than twice, that app needs a lock you cannot open. The evidence is in.
1bab8fb2: Rather than picking one model, Disconnect provides all three of the ones that work and lets you choose per rule:
e3996752: Soft lock — a reminder of why you blocked it, then you can continue. Friction, for unconscious reaching.
b1098bd5: Medium lock — a five-minute wait, and cancelling restarts the timer rather than skipping it. For restlessness that passes.
d4956b52: Hard lock — only your buddy can approve an unlock. No override, no backdoor, no setting that turns it off.
afb19cb9: All three are in the free version, including Hard lock, so the strongest option is not behind a subscription. See how this compares to other blockers.
9b678def: A lock you genuinely cannot open
0ad77304: Hard lock has no override and no backdoor. Only your buddy can approve an unlock, and approvals expire on their own.
d6be8242: Do not start with Hard lock on everything. Block your single worst app first. People who lock six apps on day one are back to zero by day ten.
89ae70ef: Set the schedule wider than feels comfortable. If the danger window is 9pm to midnight, block from 8pm. Relapse happens at the edges, in the half-hour before the rule kicks in.
